findings.claim: "The price fell from $1,200 in 1909 to just $295 by 1928" and "By 1929, Ford was producing more than one car every three minutes" (both repeated in three mark schemes and two flashcards).
findings.truth: The Model T Runabout listed at $825 in 1909 and fell to $260 in 1925; US production ended on 26 May 1927, so no Model T was sold in 1928. The three-minute interval between finished cars belongs to the Highland Park line of 1913-14, not 1929.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Ford Model T' (price table; 'on May 26, 1927, Ford Motor Company ceased US production'; 15 millionth Model T)

findings.claim: Card 2 answer "FordneyMcCumber".
findings.truth: The hyphen has been stripped from Fordney-McCumber.

findings.claim: Card 1: answer "1920s", question "The _____ Economic Boom In the 1920s, the USA saw rapid economic growth known as the 'Boom".
findings.truth: The answer sits inside its own question and the question is cut off mid-word.
findings.evidence: validator rule: an answer must not appear in its own question

findings.claim: The Fordney-McCumber Tariff "raised import duties to their highest levels".
findings.truth: It was the highest tariff to that date, but the Hawley-Smoot Tariff of 1930 (taught in Lesson 6) went higher. Worth a qualifier such as 'to their highest level yet'.

findings.claim: "This lesson covers two AQA spec points".
findings.truth: The exam board is never named in student-facing text.

findings.claim: Babe Ruth "earned $80,000 a year - more than the President", set in the 1927 season.
findings.truth: Ruth's contract for 1927-29 paid $70,000 a year, below President Coolidge's and Hoover's $75,000. He settled for $80,000 a year only in March 1930, which is when the Hoover comparison was made.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Babe Ruth' ('Having just concluded a three-year contract at an annual salary of $70,000... Ruth settling for two years at an unprecedented $80,000 per year', March 1930); Wikiquote 'Babe Ruth' (Hoover $75,000, 1930)

findings.claim: "The Hays Code set moral guidelines for films" taught as part of 1920s cinema.
findings.truth: The Production Code was adopted in 1930 and only rigidly enforced from 1 July 1934. Will Hays led the studios' own body (MPPDA) from 1922, and the 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls' list came in 1927.

findings.claim: "about 100 million Americans - out of a population of 123 million - went to the cinema every week. Almost every person in the country was visiting a movie theatre weekly."
findings.truth: 100 million is weekly admissions, not 100 million different people; regular cinema-goers went several times a week. The inference drawn is false.
findings.evidence: internal logic; standard attendance figures count tickets

findings.claim: Card 4: answer "Cultural", question "A _____ Revolution The 1920s were not just an economic boom - they were a cultural revolution".
findings.truth: The answer appears in its own question.

findings.claim: Cards 3 and 5 both answer "Volstead".
findings.truth: Two flashcards in one lesson must not share the same answer text; the deck fails the validator.

findings.claim: Card 3 question ends "any drink with more than 0"; card 4 question opens "Key Fact - The _____ Framework".
findings.truth: Both questions are cut-off fragments taken from the page furniture.

findings.claim: "Around 6 million farmers were forced off their land during the 1920s" (repeated in the key fact, the conclusion and a key takeaway), against Lesson 1's "around 600,000 farmers lost their farms".
findings.truth: The USA had only about 6.5 million farms in total in 1920, so 6 million farmers losing their land is impossible. The figure that belongs to this decade is 600,000 farmers, as Lesson 1 states; roughly 6 million people (not farmers) left the land.
findings.evidence: US Census of Agriculture farm counts; Lesson 1 of this unit

findings.claim: "Around 60% of American families lived below the poverty line" (intro, conclusion and takeaway), against Lesson 1's 42% and this lesson's own key fact.
findings.truth: 60% is the share of families earning under $2,000 a year, the income needed for a decent standard of living; 42% were below the poverty line. The lesson's own key fact states the $2,000 version correctly.
findings.evidence: Lesson 1 and Lesson 4 key fact of this unit (Brookings 1929 income study)

findings.claim: The 1921 Emergency Quota Act "Set a maximum of 375,000 immigrants per year" (repeated in a knowledge check and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Act capped annual arrivals at about 357,000 (357,803).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Emergency Quota Act' ('capped annual arrivals... at 358,000 approximately')

findings.claim: The 1929 entry: "Immigration from Asia was banned entirely" (repeated in a knowledge check).
findings.truth: Asian immigration was barred by the 1924 Johnson-Reed Act. 1929 is the year the 150,000 National Origins quota took effect.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Immigration Act of 1924' ('prevented immigration from Asia'; National Origins Formula pool of 150,000)

findings.claim: "Before he died, Parmenter described his attackers as 'slim foreigners with olive skins.'"
findings.truth: No dying statement by Frederick Parmenter is recorded. He was the unarmed paymaster, shot twice and fatally in the back while fleeing. The 'foreign-looking' identification came from eyewitnesses, and is the heart of the case against Sacco and Vanzetti.

findings.claim: Glossary and page definition: "Imperial Wizard - The title used by the leader of the Ku Klux Klan, meaning 'Imperial Wizard.'"
findings.truth: The entry defines the term with itself.

findings.claim: Card 4: answer "American", question "Around 60% of _____ families lived below the poverty line".
findings.truth: The card carries the wrong figure and tests a filler word.

findings.claim: Key takeaway: "Share values fell from $87 billion to $30 billion in weeks."
findings.truth: $30 billion was the loss, not the value left standing - the lesson body says the market 'had lost about $30 billion' by mid-November. Share values fell from about $87 billion to about $55 billion.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's own timeline

findings.claim: "Republican candidate Herbert Hoover promised Americans 'a chicken in every pot and two cars in every garage.'"
findings.truth: The line comes from a Republican National Committee newspaper advertisement of October 1928, not from Hoover himself; he never said it. I could not verify this in session (the Wikipedia pages fetched do not carry it), so I have left the text alone. Options: reattribute to 'a Republican campaign advertisement in 1928', or leave.
findings.evidence: widely documented misattribution; not verified this session

findings.claim: Glossary entry "Republican laissez-faire".
findings.truth: The term is laissez-faire; 'Republican' is the context, not part of the term. Lesson 15's glossary has it right.

findings.claim: Bonus Army: "Two veterans were killed and over 1,000 injured, including women and children. An 11-month-old baby died in the attack." (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Two veterans were shot dead by police; 55 veterans were injured and 135 arrested. The baby, Bernard Meyer, was 12 weeks old and died in hospital after the tear gas attack (a government inquiry blamed enteritis).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Bonus Army' ('55 veterans were injured and 135 arrested... 12-week-old Bernard Meyer died in the hospital')

findings.claim: Hoover "famously declaring 'Prosperity is just around the corner.'"
findings.truth: The phrase is a contemporary slogan repeatedly pinned on Hoover rather than a documented statement of his. Same call as the free-tier sibling unit, which recorded it without editing.

findings.claim: Card 5 answer "250000".
findings.truth: The comma has been stripped from 250,000.

findings.claim: Huey Long's Share Our Wealth "would cap personal fortunes at $3 million" (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Long's bill proposed a 100% tax on fortunes above $100 million; later versions of his pitch used $50 million and then $5 million. No version used $3 million. The $5,000 family income in the same sentence is right.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Share Our Wealth' ('cap personal fortunes at $100 million')

findings.claim: Roosevelt after the 1936 landslide: "He joked: 'Everyone is against the New Deal - except the voters!'"
findings.truth: No such remark by Roosevelt is on record (it does not appear in Wikiquote's sourced or attributed lists). Replaced with the verified detail: only Maine and Vermont voted for Landon.

findings.claim: "Unemployment fell from 14 million (25%) in 1933 to 7 million (14%) by 1937" (repeated in the takeaways and three mark schemes), against 13 million in Lessons 5 and 6 and in two knowledge checks.
findings.truth: The official 1933 figure is 12.8 million (24.9%); 13 million and 14 million are both in circulation in textbooks. Either make the unit consistent at 13 million - one content line, one takeaway and three mark schemes - or leave both. I have left it; a knowledge check already marks 13 million correct, so a student meeting both could be confused.

findings.claim: The CWA "was replaced by the WPA in 1935".
findings.truth: The CWA was wound up in March 1934; relief passed back to FERA before the WPA was created in 1935.

findings.claim: "boondoggles... The word came from old cowboy slang for a useless task."
findings.truth: The word comes from Scout craftwork (a braided leather cord) and entered political use in 1935; the cowboy origin is not supported.

findings.claim: Card 2 answer "FDRs".
findings.truth: The apostrophe has been stripped from FDR's, leaving a non-word.

findings.claim: "The WASPs (Women Airforce Service Pilots) were trained to deliver aircraft to war zones" (repeated in a key takeaway).
findings.truth: WASPs flew only inside the United States - ferrying new aircraft between bases, towing targets and testing repaired planes. None flew to a war zone.

findings.claim: The Tuskegee Airmen "flew over 15,000 missions" (repeated in three mark schemes).
findings.truth: The 15,000 figure counts individual combat sorties, not missions. Same correction as the free-tier sibling unit.

findings.claim: "By the end of the 1930s, the first colour films appeared, including The Wizard of Oz (1939)."
findings.truth: Colour features pre-date the late 1930s: Becky Sharp (1935) was the first full three-strip Technicolor feature, and two-colour processes ran through the 1920s.

findings.claim: "The iconic 'Rosie the Riveter' - a strong woman in overalls flexing her bicep with the slogan 'We Can Do It!' - became the symbol of women's wartime contribution."
findings.truth: Two different images are merged. 'We Can Do It!' was an internal Westinghouse morale poster by J. Howard Miller (1943), not a government recruitment campaign, and was only identified with 'Rosie' from the 1980s. Rosie the Riveter is Norman Rockwell's 1943 Saturday Evening Post cover.
findings.evidence: standard art history of both images

findings.claim: "The Korean War (1951) was another boost" (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Korean War ran from June 1950 to July 1953, as the unit's own Lesson 10 says.

findings.claim: "each identical house could be built in just 16 minutes per stage" (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: 16 minutes was the interval between completed houses at peak (about 30 a day), not the time per stage. Same correction as the free-tier sibling unit.
findings.evidence: sibling unit finding F37; Wikipedia 'Levittown, New York'

findings.claim: "Levittown's contracts explicitly banned sales to African Americans. This practice, known as 'redlining'..." (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: A clause in a deed banning a sale is a restrictive covenant. Redlining is the separate practice of banks and insurers refusing lending in areas mapped as Black.

findings.claim: "the first McDonald's in 1955" (repeated in a knowledge check).
findings.truth: The McDonald brothers opened their first restaurant in 1940; 1955 is Ray Kroc's first franchise in Des Plaines.

findings.claim: Truman quoted as: "Every segment of our population has a right to expect from his government a fair deal."
findings.truth: The 1949 State of the Union wording is 'Every segment of our population and every individual has a right to expect from our Government a fair deal.'

findings.claim: Card 3 answer "PostWar".
findings.truth: The hyphen has been stripped from Post-war.

findings.claim: "Two wartime allies - China and the USSR - were now hostile nuclear powers." (1950)
findings.truth: China tested its first atomic bomb in 1964. In 1950 only the USSR had the bomb, from August 1949.
findings.evidence: nuclear chronology; the lesson's own takeaway dates the Soviet bomb to 1949

findings.claim: The federal loyalty programme "around 6.6 million government workers were investigated" (repeated in a knowledge check and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: The programme investigated over 3 million employees, and 'by mid-1952, more than 4 million people, actual or prospective employees, had gone through the check'. The lesson's dismissal figure (about 500) is in range (300-560).

findings.claim: "Hoover called King the 'most dangerous Negro in America'."
findings.truth: The phrase is from an FBI memo by William Sullivan (1963): King is 'the most dangerous Negro of the future in this Nation'. Hoover's own documented insult was 'the most notorious liar in the country'.
findings.evidence: FBI Sullivan memo; not verified this session

findings.claim: Two definitions are cut off at 'Plessy v.' - the 'separate but equal' entry and the Brown v. Board entry - and the same truncation appears in two page definitions and two flashcards.
findings.truth: The sentence splitter broke on 'v.' The full name is Plessy v. Ferguson (1896).

findings.claim: Card 2 answer '"separate but equal,"' carries a trailing comma inside the quotation marks.
findings.truth: The stray comma was pulled in with the term.

findings.claim: The Woolworth's entry begins "A Woolworth's department store in Greensboro...", so the flashcard built from it puts the answer inside its own question.
findings.truth: The entry defines the term with itself.

findings.claim: Card 4 answer "SitIn".
findings.truth: The hyphen has been stripped from sit-in.

findings.claim: Glossary entry "congressional politics - Lyndon Johnson was famous for his ability to persuade, pressure, and charm members of Congress into supporting his legislation."
findings.truth: The entry describes Johnson instead of defining the term.

findings.claim: King quoted as saying the Great Society had been "shot down on the battlefields of Vietnam" (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: King's 1967 wording is singular: 'shot down on the battlefield of Vietnam'.

findings.claim: The poverty diagram's alt text gives poverty falling from 19% to 11.1%, against the lesson body's 22% to 13%.
findings.truth: Two different series (all persons vs families, and different base years). The alt text is not read by most students but it does not match the page.

findings.claim: "They used confrontational tactics - burning bras, disrupting the Miss World pageant..."
findings.truth: The American protest was at the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City in September 1968, where bras, girdles and mops went into a 'freedom trash can'; nothing was set alight. The Miss World protest was London, November 1970.

findings.claim: "Schlafly was both a housewife and a qualified lawyer" while founding STOP ERA in 1972.
findings.truth: Schlafly took her law degree in 1978, six years after STOP ERA began. She had run for Congress in 1952 and 1970, as the text says.

findings.claim: The lesson dates Reed v. Reed to 1971; the specification lists 'the Supreme Court ruling on equal rights (1972)'.
findings.truth: Reed v. Reed was decided on 22 November 1971, so the lesson is right and the spec's date is loose. Either add a line noting that some sources date it 1972, or leave it. The free-tier sibling unit raised the same point. I have left it.
findings.evidence: spec section AD part three; Reed v. Reed judgment date

findings.claim: "This is the central question of the AQA unit" and "This tension is at the heart of the AQA specification."
findings.truth: The exam board is never named in student-facing text.

findings.claim: Across all 15 lessons the flashcard decks are machine-generated: roughly 45 of the 75 cards are cloze fragments cut out of headings ('_____ Inequality Beneath the Boom Not everyone shared...', 'The _____ of Cinema Cinema became...'), and about 28 are bare glossary definitions with no question stem.
findings.truth: Only the cards that are factually wrong, duplicated, mangled or self-answering are fixed here (30 edits). The deck as a whole needs a rebuild to the house standard - a real question stem, and 'Which word means...?' on definition-front cards - which is a separate job from a fact-check.

findings.claim: Fourteen of the fifteen lesson descriptions run over 100 characters (L1 124, L12 143, L15 147); only Lesson 4 is inside the limit.
findings.truth: The house validator caps a lesson description at 100 characters. Nothing here is factually wrong, and I have not rewritten them, but the unit will trip that check if it is revalidated.

summary: Fifteen lessons checked against the spec's option AD content list and its assessment section: the period study is six compulsory questions worth 4/4/8/4/8/12 with no SPaG marks in this section, and every practice question in the unit matches that pattern, so the exam framing is sound. No banned band names, no invented examiner claims and no fabricated mark-scheme wording. The breaches are elsewhere: one HIGH (a dying statement invented for the murdered paymaster in the Sacco and Vanzetti case), three places that name the exam board to students, and a run of wrong figures - the Model T at $1,200/$295, Babe Ruth's salary and the Hoover comparison moved to 1927, the Hays Code taught as 1920s, 6 million farmers off the land, 60% below the poverty line, the 1921 quota at 375,000, the Asian ban dated 1929, 1,000 Bonus Army injured and an 11-month-old baby, Huey Long's $3 million cap, an unsourced Roosevelt quip, WASPs flying to war zones, 15,000 Tuskegee 'missions', the Korean War dated 1951, Levittown's 16 minutes per stage, restrictive covenants called redlining, China as a nuclear power in 1950, 6.6 million loyalty checks and a bra-burning at Miss World. 87 edits. Three ADJUDICATE items and fifteen notes; no lesson was completely clean.
